variants.text: I administered a second course of Prednisone on August 3 after the patient lost hearing in the right ear. I am prescribing 60mg for three days, then tapering down to one pill on August 28. The previous physician used a lower dose and shorter schedule. The patient gained 15 pounds of fluid. The patient consumes more calories and seeks sugar despite taking a glp-1 medication. The patient's abdomen protrudes outward. I am reading clinical literature on dietary adjustments and sleep cycle regulation. The patient is scheduled to return to baseline metrics within two months. I am sharing this clinical data with you. You can read other patient experiences and coping methods by doing a general search for Prednisone weight gain.

I'm on my second course of Prednisone since Aug 3 when I woke up totally deaf in my right ear.

I am taking a higher amount
(60mg for another 3 days, and then gradually tapering down to 1 last pill on Aug 28th).

The first ENT I saw didn't prescribe a high enough dose, or long enough schedule.

I've now gained 15lbs (of water weight mostly).

There's been some sugar cravings, and my calories have increased even with me being on a glp-1.

It's been seriously tough on me to feel my gut balloon out!

I just keep researching the best ways to eat and manage my mood/sleep cycle, hoping I return to my baseline within a couple of months.

My heart is with you.

Keep looking into others experiences and how they cope, and it will provide some needed insight.

You can just do a general search for Prednisone weight gain, etc.

Since August 3rd, when I woke up deaf in my right ear, I have been on my second course of Prednisone. Today I take the final 1mg pill, completing the taper schedule that began with 60mg for 3 days. The first ENT prescribed a lower dose and shorter schedule. I have gained 15lbs, mostly from water retention. I am eating more sugary foods, and my daily caloric intake has gone up even while taking a glp-1 medication. My abdomen is visibly distended. I am researching dietary adjustments and sleep cycle protocols, tracking my physical state until my measurements return to baseline over the next couple of months. You can type "Prednisone weight gain" into a search engine to read how others navigate these physical changes.

I have worn hearing aids for 35 years. I scheduled an appointment and acquired a $7,000 pair of Fortell devices. I reviewed the return policy and kept the receipt. I packed the devices in my carry-on bag and flew from San Diego to New York. I visited my daughter. During the visit, I wore the new devices in loud bars and restaurants. I activated their noise-cancellation and AI speech-focus modes. I observed the sound levels around me. 

I compared these functions to my previous Oticon aids, which sat in their case on the hotel nightstand. I noted the decibel changes across different frequencies during the conversations. I tracked the differences in sound reception between the two brands. I logged the battery life and the physical fit of the plastic molds in my ear canals. 

I participated in Fortell's remote service model for device adjustments. I ran the tuning software using my computer microphone. After five days, I placed the $7,000 aids in their original box. I wrote a return label and dropped the package at the post office. I unpacked my Oticon aids and placed them back in my ears. 

Before starting this process, I wrote a list of ten specific hearing environments and the required acoustic outputs for each. I gathered the published

I have worn hearing aids for thirty-five years. The brain adjusts to the devices over time, and any equipment change triggers a physical acclimatization period. I went to the clinic and acquired a pair of the new models. I paid seven thousand dollars for the devices.

I traveled from San Diego to New York. I visited my daughter and scheduled an appointment with the provider there. I brought the devices with me on the trip. I kept the return receipt in my travel bag during the flight.

I activated the noise-cancellation and speech-focus AI modes in loud bars and restaurants in New York. The devices stayed in my ears during those conversations. After the trip, I packed the devices back into their case and returned them to the clinic before the trial period ended. I placed my previous Oticon aids back into my ears.

Hearing loss involves shifting decibel levels across different frequencies, requiring periodic equipment adjustments. The manufacturer operates through a remote service model. I sat at my desk in San Diego while a technician adjusted my Oticon aids through a computer connection. We ran through the frequency band settings on the screen.

I wrote a list of ten specific hearing environments and the target audio output for each. I compared the technical specifications and the published study results between the two manufacturers. I filed the papers, returned the loaner equipment, and ended the trial.

For me, there was not one moment when my hearing changed. There were repeated incidents at the counter and in the back room. I asked customers to repeat orders when the grinder was running. I watched the mouths of people speaking across the counter. I turned the radio volume higher until the sound reached the storage room, then lowered it after someone pointed to the dial. Sometimes a person said something, I said "what?", and then answered before the person spoke again. After several such exchanges, I visited a clinic, sat in a booth, and wore headphones while tones played. Later, I placed a device behind my ear and asked whether other workers had visited clinics.

Last year I lay in an MRI machine for SSHL at a clinic, then sat in the waiting room while the results were reviewed. A CT scan and lab tests followed. The results were normal, and the cause of my SSHL was not identified.

For me, I don't think there was one dramatic moment where I suddenly realized I couldn't hear anymore.

It was more like a bunch of little things that kept happening.

I'd ask people to repeat themselves, especially if there was background noise.

I'd find myself watching someone's face while they were talking because I was trying to fill in the words I didn't catch.

I'd turn the TV up and then realize it was probably louder than everyone else wanted it to be.

And sometimes someone would say something, I'd say "what?" and then understand them a second later without them even repeating it.

Looking back, I think that was the point when I started taking my hearing loss more seriously.

I'm curious what it was like for other people?

There was no single night when the museum doors began opening without a key.

It came as a set of small events across the galleries.

I radioed the front desk twice during each round, especially when the ventilation system was running.

I stood in front of the portrait cases while the guard beside me spoke; the sentences arrived in fragments.

I raised the thermostat in the office and then saw the dial above the red mark.

Sometimes an alarm would sound, I would say, "what?" and the hallway lights would come on a second later without anyone touching the panel.

After the third incident, I began checking each lock with a paper list.

I left a note asking how the night rounds had been recorded at other museums.

Last month, my sister had an MRI for SSHL and returned for the results and received a normal report. A CT scan and several labs were completed too, and each result was normal. The cause of her SSHL remains unidentified.
I record the MRI, CT scan, and lab results for patients with sudden hearing loss. The images show no abnormalities. The charts note that the cause of each hearing loss remains unidentified.

In my office, one distinct moment seldom occurs when a patient's hearing changes. More often, a series of separate events comes up during the intake form. Patients report asking people to repeat themselves, especially when a room has background noise. They describe watching a speaker's face while the person talks. They mention turning the television volume higher, and people in the next room call out. Sometimes a patient says "what?" and then answers before the other person repeats the sentence. When these examples appear on several visits, I schedule a hearing test and discuss the results. I ask patients to describe the sequence.

I got a MRI last year for SSHL and thought it was gonna be bad but I came back normal thank goodness. They did a CT scan also and some labs. Everything came back normal. The bad part is they dont know what caused my SSHL.

A CT scan and lab work were done too, and all results were normal. Thank goodness, my MRI last year for SSHL was normal, though I expected bad news. The frustrating part is they don't know what caused my SSHL.

It has been 6 days since the tympanoplasty procedure. The ear drum perforation repair proceeded without intraoperative events. I replaced the external ear packing on two occasions this week following fluid drainage from the canal. I administered over-the-counter analgesic tablets during the afternoon intervals. Tomorrow is the 1-week post-operative clinic visit. I will outline the timeline for fluid cessation and analgesic weaning, and define the physiological thresholds for clinical intervention.

Tomorrow is my one-week postoperative appointment. Six days have passed since my eardrum perforation repair, an uncomplicated tympanoplasty without any prior or intraoperative issues. Still, I've needed to swap the outer ear dressing two times because it was soaked with heavy drainage. Although my discomfort has lessened drastically, it spikes daily in the afternoon, compelling me to use non-prescription analgesics. When should I start worrying? For how much longer are the drainage and aches supposed to persist?

I am interested in how this experience was for others. In retrospect, I believe those minor indications marked the moment I began treating my hearing loss more seriously. For me, I do not believe there was a single striking instant when I abruptly understood that I could no longer hear. Instead, many small episodes continued to occur. I would increase the television volume, then recognize it was probably louder than others desired. I often requested that people say things again, particularly when ambient sound was present. I would observe a speaker's face while they talked, trying to supply the words I had missed. Occasionally, someone would speak, I would say "what?", and a moment later I would comprehend them even though they had not repeated themselves.

It has been 6 days since my tympanoplasty surgery.

There was no complication during or before the surgery, just a simple ear drum perforation repair.

However, it has been 6 days since the operation, and I have had to change the external ear packing twice as it was stained with significant discharge.

Pain has gone significantly down, but it still peaks in the afternoon, which forces me to take OTC pain meds.

How long is the discharge and pain expected to be there?
When should I be concerned??

My 1 week post op visit is tomorrow.

I move my fingers behind my ears and the base of my skull. My husband made these exact motions a year ago. He now sits across the room, turning the pages of a newspaper. Two voices speak from near the ceiling. Sometimes they yell. My husband shakes his head when I point at the corner. A high-pitched tone rings in my left ear, and I press my palm flat against it. I hear the two voices speaking to each other. When I walk toward the humming desk fan, the voices become louder. I turn the fan's dial to a higher speed. The voices raise their volume. I step back toward the wall, and their words fade. My husband turns a small dial on his wristwatch, and the voices stop entirely for a minute. I turn the fan off and on. The voices remain at a steady volume. I walk to the window and speak a single sentence aloud. The two voices repeat the exact words back to me. I type this out on my keyboard, hitting the keys one by one.

I sit in the vehicle outside the residence. I adjust the frequency dial on the transmitter. On the monitor, the man raises his arms, moving his fingers behind his head and ears. I speak into the microphone. The woman pauses near the living room fan and tilts her head. I increase the pitch slider. The woman touches her left ear. The man paces the floor, shaking his head. I press the button to emit the high-frequency tone. The woman steps closer to the wall. I turn the volume knob down. The man lowers his hands. I switch the channel. The woman moves away from the wall. I record their spoken words on the hard drive. I watch them through the camera feed. The man rubs his ears. The woman stands by the fan. I transmit two distinct voices through the speaker system. The man waves his arms. The woman writes on a notepad. I log the timestamp and shut down the terminal.

Around twelve months back, I observed my spouse beginning to make odd gestures with his hands and digits behind his skull and ears. He insists there's nothing inside his ear causing this. At the exact same period, I began detecting an extremely elevated ringing tone in my ears, and my left ear now seems obstructed. I distinctly perceive two individuals conversing. Occasionally I comprehend their words, other times they yell at him and I detect it crystal clear. I also pick up on these two voices, though not quite as distinctly as he does. I believe they can detect me too, but here's the peculiar aspect. When I approach a fan or a wall or something similar, I pick them up more clearly. It appears to be some sort of advanced technology, but I'm unable to comprehend it. He can adjust his volume up and down, whereas I cannot manage that I lack such capability. I've attempted every possible solution. I suspect it's merely surveillance equipment monitoring me and capturing my conversations, though I'm not certain. Could someone please assist?

In my school district, children with hearing loss receive hearing aids during the first term, and ASL classes are scheduled after follow-up checks. Some students use signs from the start. Others practice spoken language with aids. Teachers record which students respond to sound and which use signs during lessons. Parents attend meetings where communication plans are written. Interpreters are assigned for classrooms, and students practice conversations with staff who use ASL and with staff who do not.

I grew up in a deaf school where ASL was used in every class. Now I teach ASL to hearing children at a community center. Their parents attend evening sessions and practice signs at home. The children use hearing aids during speech lessons, then switch to signing during group activities. Some children use both methods in the same hour. Outside the classroom, they order food, ask for directions, and introduce themselves to neighbors with signs and spoken words.

At my school, each child receives a hearing test, and the results set the schedule. Some children attend ASL classes after being fitted with hearing aids. Others begin ASL sessions only after weeks of using the aids during school hours. Teachers demonstrate signs beside the student desks. Parents practice spoken language at home. Outside the school, neighbors, shopkeepers, and bus drivers use spoken language, and the children respond to them with gestures, writing, or speech.

I agree with you… the degree of loss and frequency is different for everyone.
Asl should be taught accordingly.
Many hoh of course need it.
No denyin.
But.. let them get used to hearing aids first.
And if they are still struggling, then asl of course.
Or else yes, kids will learn to only asl.
And sadly many regular people do not know asl.
And wont be able to communicate with him or her.
Cause, there is obviously a world to deal with outside the deaf community.

About eight months ago my roommate began making these repetitive gestures with his hands near his neck and jaw, moving his fingers around for minutes at a time. I hear two voices speaking. Sometimes the words come through clearly, other times they shout at him and I hear every word. He says nothing is in his ear. Around the same period I started getting a sharp ringing in my right ear and it has become blocked on that side. I also hear those same two voices. Not as loud as he does but they come through. When I stand close to the refrigerator or the air conditioner or any running machine the voices get louder. He can make his louder or quieter by moving his fingers near his jaw. I have not been able to do that with mine no matter what I try. The voices respond when I speak. Can someone please help with this.

Okay, so I noticed about a year ago that my husband started doing these weird motions with his arms and his fingers behind his head and his ears. I can clearly hear two people talking; sometimes I get what they're saying, sometimes they scream at him, and I can hear it plain as day. He swears there's nothing in his ear. Doing this at the same time, he got his thing. I also started noticing a very, very high pitch in my ears, and my left ear is now what feels like blocked.

I also hear these two people—not as clearly as him, but pretty clear. I think they can hear me as well, but here's the strange part: if I go near a fan or a wall—something of that nature—I can hear them better.

It's some kind of new technology, but I can't figure it out. He can turn his up and down; I can't seem to do that. I don't have that ability. I've tried everything. I think it is just spy on me and things that I'm saying, but not sure. Can anybody please help?

I’m with you… since there is clearly a world to handle beyond the deaf community, many typical individuals don’t know ASL and won’t be able to converse with him or her. Each person’s severity and frequency of loss vary, so ASL ought to be taught in a fitting way. Plenty of hard-of-hearing folks certainly require it, undoubtedly. However… allow them to adjust to hearing aids first. If they continue having difficulty, then ASL naturally. Otherwise, indeed, children will end up relying solely on ASL.

At the start of this term I resumed wearing hearing aids after several years without them. During the previous term I enrolled in a course taught by a professor whose speech moved slowly and paused between phrases. I sat near the front, watched the professor’s mouth, and took notes from the board. When the lectures ended, I met two classmates in the library, compared their notes with mine, and copied sections absent from my notebook. I also opened the course page, downloaded the slides, and read the assigned chapters. The final grade came from written work and a take-home exam.

This term my schedule lists two courses with the same professor. One of them meets in a small room with two other students and me. The syllabus says participation counts toward the grade, and the professor assigns discussion prompts, paired questions, and short spoken responses. During the first meeting, the professor looked at each student in turn, waited for answers, and asked follow-up questions. I kept my notebook open, wrote down the questions, and answered after the professor finished speaking.

I have begun wearing the hearing aids during shifts at work. The office has several desks close together, phones ring, printers run, and people talk across partitions. At lunch I sit near two coworkers while they speak. I turn my head toward them, watch their faces, and keep my hands still on the table. The hearing aids increase the sound from their voices. I write some words in my notepad and leave other lines blank. When they speak quickly, I look at their mouths. When they pause, I write a few words in the margin of my notepad. If they continue talking, I remain seated and keep my eyes on the speaker. If one of them asks me a question, I repeat the last words spoken before answering.

After work I place the hearing aids in their case, wipe them with a cloth, and set the case beside my laptop. In the evening I open the course portal, check messages from the professor, and review the discussion questions for the next session. I also schedule a meeting with the accessibility office and bring the hearing aids, the class schedule, and a list of the rooms where the courses meet.

Recently I’ve started using my hearing aids again after several year of no use.
The main reason of me not using them its because the overall hearing loss is not serious enough (for me) to justify use them in daily life.
I would have trouble hearing specific people or social situations, but it would never be that much of a hassle (trash excuse to hide the fact that I hate how noisy life gets).
Last semester, had a proff which had speech impediment that caused her speech to be very slow and halting.
had trouble hearing her throughout the entire semester but somehow managed to pass the class not relaying on lectures but classmates and info online.
New semester start, I had to take TWO courses with her, and in one of them it will be hard to hide the fact that I can't hear her, since there are only three of us in total and the interaction will be more one-on-one.
Decided to use hearing aids again to check if its helps to any degree.
still hadn’t any lectures with her yet, but so far I’ve been using them on my work.
One thing Ive noticed so far is i still have trouble trying to understand or make up what ppl are saying.
Yes I hear things louder, but it feels that it doesn’t necessarily make speech more clear for me.
ive been trying to eavesdrop (lol) some coworkers to test my hearing improvement, but it feels like although I can “hear” the sound they’re making I can’t really make out every word they say, and every time I tried harder to listen every syllable the less I could understand their convo.

Don’t know if im not processing stuff the way im supposed to or my expectations of how hearing aids works are way off.
I’ve been thinking maybe im overwhelmed by all the noise that im suddenly hearing and how loud everything is, but I don’t know if you’re capable to get used to it and “adjust” volume levels (as you’re naturally supposed to).

Idk if anyone have any advice on the matter or there are some stuff I should be doing :(

After several years, I began wearing hearing aids again while working as a lab assistant. The audiogram lists thresholds above 25 decibels. In certain conversations I asked people to repeat sentences, then continued without them. Last term, a lecturer spoke slowly because of a speech impediment. I attended her sessions, copied the slides, borrowed recordings, and used online materials. I passed the course. This term, I am assigned to two sessions led by the same lecturer, and one session has three participants seated around a small table. Each participant answers questions directly. I took the hearing aids from their case and put them in before work. I have not yet attended her sessions. During shifts, I wear them while sorting samples and entering records. Coworkers speak nearby. I turn my head toward them, watch their mouths, and ask them to repeat phrases. The sound reaches me at a higher volume. The words do not separate into syllables at the same rate. I stand near the break room and listen to two technicians discuss a schedule. I mark the rhythm and some vowels. When I lean forward and watch their mouths, my notes contain blank spaces. I adjust the volume button, move to rooms with closed doors, and keep the aids in for several hours. I carry a small notebook in my pocket. I mark the times when the aids are on. I have scheduled an appointment with the clinic. I bring a list of rooms, distances, and background sounds. I write down the names of people speaking during handovers. I ask colleagues to face me during handovers. I use captions on training videos and request written summaries. I practice repeating sentences aloud after recordings. I place the aids on the charger at night. I still wear the aids each morning.

Recently I began using a lapel microphone again after several semesters without one. My speech has remained slow and halting since therapy ended, and the department assigned me a classroom with a small round table. Last term I taught one section with twelve students. I stood near the whiteboard and repeated each sentence twice. A student in the front row used hearing aids and took notes from the slides. During office hours, two other students attended, and I wrote key terms on index cards. This term I teach two sections. One section meets in a room with three chairs arranged facing each other. The roster lists the same student, and the syllabus requires weekly spoken responses. I placed the microphone on the table and tested the recording system before the first meeting. Before that meeting, I used the microphone in the department office while colleagues answered phones and printers ran nearby. The device raised the volume of my voice and captured the sound of papers, keyboard taps, and the ventilation system. In the hallway afterward, I replayed the file and counted the words that were separated by background noise. I also asked two coworkers to read a list of terms at a set pace while I wore the earpiece connected to the microphone. They read the list twice, and I wrote down each word on a clipboard. On the third pass, I asked them to pause between phrases. The written list contained gaps where the consonants overlapped with the fan noise. I scheduled another session with the campus accessibility office and brought the microphone, the recording, and the list. The technician adjusted the gain, changed the windscreen, and ran a speech-in-noise test with sentences played through a speaker. I repeated the sentences aloud and marked the lines that appeared on the printed transcript. The office sent a memo to the registrar about seating placement, and I copied the student on the message.

I’m 36 and bought hearing aids last spring. I keep a notebook and use text messages during conversations. My partner repeats sentences and writes down addresses. I attend appointments with an audiologist. The devices pick up sound in quiet rooms, but not in crowded rooms, so I face the speaker and ask people to type.

I’m 41, and I use captioning on every phone call and meeting. I visited an audiology clinic last month and had two devices fitted. They amplify voices, doorbells, and alarms, and I read captions during conversations. I keep a notebook by the desk, ask people to write dates and addresses, and reread messages before answering. At home, subtitles stay on, and I face the speaker whenever the light allows.

if it makes you feel bettter, I’m 34 and paid a lot of money for hearing aids…and I understand even less than your husband.
I literally can’t do anything but rely on text comunication.
he should go to an audiologist but hearing aids doňt work for everyone.
they give me access to sound but hearing doesn’t mean understanding.
the clarity just isn’t there

I am 61 and fit hearing devices in a clinic. I review test charts, place receivers in ears, and adjust volume controls. I hand clients written instructions, schedule follow-up visits, and note which sounds are detected in each session. I use captions on videos, face the window during conversations, and keep a notepad beside the keyboard.

He ought to see an audiologist, though hearing aids aren’t effective for everybody. I truly can do nothing except depend on written messages. Maybe this helps, but I’m 34 and spent heavily on hearing aids, yet I comprehend even less than your husband. They let me reach sound, but hearing isn’t the same as understanding; the clearness simply isn’t present.

After several years of leaving them unused, I’ve lately begun wearing my hearing aids once more. So far, I’ve mainly been keeping them in while working, although I haven’t yet had any sessions with the instructor who prompted this. This term I’m enrolled in two classes taught by the same professor I had last term. She has a speech impediment that makes her delivery slow and halting, and I had difficulty hearing her throughout the whole previous term. Even so, I managed to pass by leaning on classmates and online material rather than relying on her lectures. Now, though, one of the courses will make it much harder to mask my difficulty hearing, because only three people are involved and the interaction will be closer to one-on-one. That is why I decided to try the aids again, just to see whether they help at all.

The primary reason I had stopped wearing them was that my general hearing loss never seemed severe enough to require them in everyday life. I might struggle with particular voices or social settings, but it never felt like enough of a burden. Honestly, that is a weak excuse covering the fact that I dislike how noisy life becomes.

What I’ve noticed is that sounds are louder, yet speech does not necessarily become clearer. I still have trouble understanding or filling in what people say. I’ve even been quietly eavesdropping, haha, on coworkers to test whether my hearing has improved. I can detect the sounds they make, but I cannot catch every word. The harder I try to follow each syllable, the less I comprehend their conversation. Maybe I’m overwhelmed by the sudden noise and loudness. I’m unsure whether I’m not processing things as I should, or whether my expectations of hearing aids are far off. I wonder whether someone can get accustomed to it and mentally adjust volume levels. If anyone has advice or knows what I should be doing, I’d appreciate it :(

It's no surprise you're drained pushing yourself to function like a hearing person. Your capability does not depend on your hearing level, so embrace your intelligence and brilliance, and begin seeking additional assistance and methods that genuinely let you contribute more effortlessly.

Having perused everything, yes, this will persist unless you alter your perspective. I advise taking these steps:

* Study sign language **immediately**.
* Educate yourself on your legal rights and workplace accommodations, and secure backing so you can perform your duties with less exhaustion.
* Visit a hearing specialist for suitable assistance with auditory devices or a cochlear implant. Appropriate tech is essential, possibly including Roger mics and a Roger table microphone for your job.
* Connect with fellow Deaf and Hard of Hearing individuals. Crucial for self-worth and acquiring actionable ideas for managing tasks and self-advocacy abilities.
* Seek counseling. This is likely critical, as you evidently require assistance and techniques for managing this.

I book weekly appointments with a counselor to discuss communication methods. I attend monthly gatherings with other Deaf and Hard of Hearing individuals to exchange workplace navigation tactics. I scheduled an appointment with an audiologist to calibrate my cochlear implant, and I now set up Roger table microphones on the conference table during staff meetings. I submitted a written request to human resources for assistive technology, live captioning software, and modified break schedules. I review the written transcripts of all meetings and print out the agendas before the discussions begin. I enrolled in a sign language course at the local community center, attending three evening sessions each week. I replaced verbal phone calls with text-based communication. I complete my tasks by using visual project boards and typed summaries. I submit my project reports through the shared digital workspace. I also document my daily routines in a logbook.

After my mother began losing hearing, phone calls at her apartment followed a new routine. The caller’s voice came through the receiver without a face, a mouth, or a room to point at objects. During visits, she watched the speaker’s hands and eyebrows, and replied after each pause. On calls, she placed the handset down, let the ring stop, and wrote down messages from the voicemail later. She handed the phone to me when a clinic or bank called. Once she received hearing aids, she answered calls at the kitchen counter, repeated addresses aloud, and ended conversations without passing the receiver to me.

Only after my mother began dealing with hearing loss did I truly realize how much telephone conversations differ. Without facial cues, lipreading, or contextual clues, calls were especially hard, so she sometimes let them go to voicemail and asked another person to listen instead. In-person discussions were sometimes workable because she could watch the speaker. Once she received hearing aids, regaining the ability to manage phone calls independently was among the things she valued most, and it left her feeling delighted.

I sit at a desk with a headset and a keyboard. A captioning program opens on my monitor when a call comes in. I traveled from San Diego to NY to see my daughter, so I made an appointment. I told myself that I could return them, so I didn't feel the $7K was at risk.

I kept the aids due to their noise-cancellation and speech-focus in AI mode. And I could tell that my brain-body was better, as I didn't even notice that my aids were in. I also kept the aids, as my 10% did get better at Fortell's forte: hearing conversations in loud bars and restaurants. They are way better than my Oticon aids (that cost me about the same).

If you are a hearing aid user, you know that correcting hearing loss is more of an art than a science, given the changing nature of hearing loss (dB changes across frequencies). I feel Fortell is making it more of a science. Their service model is basically remote for me, and to my surprise, it has worked out fine.

I suggest writing down your top 10 problems and what would satisfy you in the hunt for new aids. It sounds like proven studies between hearing aid manufacturers is a top priority. Good luck in your journey.
